# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Why this book when an LLM can already 'do it'?

To illustrate the situation this book addresses, consider a
graduate biostatistics student in April 2026 who needs some
code written. She has two options. She can open a browser,
type 'bootstrap a 95% confidence interval for the median of
this data', and receive working R code in under ten seconds.
Alternatively, she can open a coding agent in her terminal
and describe the same task. The agent will then write the
function, run it, and report the result directly in her
project. In either case the code will usually run, and it
will often be correct. Unfortunately, it will sometimes be
wrong in subtle and dangerous ways that the student is not
equipped to detect.

That last possibility is the premise of the book. We do not
hold that large language models are bad. They are
remarkable tools, and to ignore them in a statistics
curriculum would be a pedagogical failure. Nor do we hold
that statisticians should refuse to use them. We assume,
and we encourage, the daily use of LLMs and coding agents
in statistical computing work. We note, however, that the
usefulness of an LLM to a biostatistician is limited by the
statistician's own ability to verify, critique, and extend
what the LLM produces. That ability must be built through
training that does not treat the LLM as a substitute for
learning.

It is our view that the student who learns the material in
this book will use LLMs more effectively than the student
who does not. The book teaches a little prompt engineering
at the end of each chapter. The advantage, however, comes
from the statistical and computational judgment that LLM
output *requires* from a human reviewer.

## What this book is not

This book is not:

- A textbook that pretends LLMs do not exist. A
  curriculum designed as if 2019 were still the current
  year trains students for a workplace that has ceased to
  exist.
- A textbook about LLMs as such. Prompt engineering,
  fine-tuning, and the engineering internals of language
  models are separate subjects, and they are covered better
  elsewhere.
- An argument that students should skip the hard parts of
  statistical computing because the LLM will handle them.
  The arrival of LLMs has *raised* the bar for what human
  statisticians must know. That is, deciding whether the
  LLM is right is now the statistician's core contribution.

The book takes a middle path. We teach statistical computing
as it has always been taught. We add a consciously
integrated treatment of where the human statistician
contributes and where the work can be delegated to the LLM.

## How this book earns its subtitle

Three structural features distinguish the book from its
predecessors, and together they carry the 'in the Age of AI'
framing.

1. **Front-loaded consciousness-raising.** Each content
   chapter opens, after the orientation, with a section
   titled *The statistician's contribution*. That section
   names the two to five decisions about the chapter's
   topic that cannot be delegated to an LLM without human
   input. Is this method appropriate? What is the data
   structure? Which variant of the procedure applies?
   These sections are short (roughly one printed page
   each), and the rest of each chapter builds on them.

2. **Adversarial LLM practice.** Each chapter closes with
   a section titled *Collaborating with an LLM on
   [topic]*. The section contains three prompts that have
   been deliberately constructed to expose common failure
   modes. Each prompt is paired with a **Verification**
   step, which tells the reader what to check and how. In
   this way the prompts train the reader to catch the
   errors that LLMs do not catch themselves.

3. **Verification-first pedagogy throughout.** Every
   non-trivial code example is paired with a concrete way
   to check the answer. The check may be a closed-form
   result, an alternative implementation, a simulation, or
   a unit test. Where code cannot be verified, we say so.

In addition, the book inherits the structural conventions
of the Posit book family [@wickham2023r4ds; @wickham2019advr;
@wickham2023rpkgs]:

- A three-question *Prerequisites* quiz at the start of
  each chapter (in the style of *Advanced R*), with
  answers at the foot of the chapter.
- *Check your understanding* collapsible callouts,
  distributed through the content as paced comprehension
  prompts.
- A *Further reading* section that curates the best next
  sources.

## Positioning against other books

A reader entering graduate biostatistics has many good
statistical computing texts to choose from. This book does
not replace any of them. Rather, it fills a gap that has
opened in the past three years.

- *Advanced R* [@wickham2019advr] and *R for Data Science*
  [@wickham2023r4ds] teach R itself superbly. However, they
  predate widespread LLM use and do not address the
  human-LLM division of labor. We recommend reading them
  alongside this one.
- *Statistical Computing with R* [@rizzo2019computing]
  covers the algorithms in more depth than this book. It
  also predates LLM integration, and it is longer and more
  mathematical. The reader who wants the theory should
  consult it.
- The Posit book family on specific tools (*ggplot2*,
  *Mastering Shiny*, *R Packages*) remains the reference
  for those tools, and this book cites them.
- *Statistical Rethinking* [@mcelreath2020rethinking] is
  the best current introduction to Bayesian computation.
  The Bayesian chapter of this book (@sec-bayesian) is
  intended as an entry point to it.

What this book adds is a unifying pedagogical framework for
statistical computing *in the presence of competent LLMs*.
We carry that framework through Parts I to X.

## Prerequisites

Readers should have:

- Completed a one-quarter course in mathematical
  statistics at the level of Casella and Berger.
- Basic familiarity with linear algebra (vectors,
  matrices, eigenvalues).
- Access to R 4.4+ and RStudio (or another IDE of their
  choosing).

We assume no prior experience with R or Git. Some prior
exposure to an LLM or a coding agent (ChatGPT, Claude,
Gemini, Claude Code, or similar) is helpful but not
required.

## Conventions

The reader is referred to the [Conventions](conventions.qmd)
page for the visual cues used throughout the book.

## How this book relates to its siblings

This book is one of three in a graduate sequence.

- [*Biostatistics Practicum*](https://rgtlab.org/practicum)
  covers the workflow that surrounds the methods:
  reproducibility, Git, Docker, renv, Quarto reporting,
  tidyverse data wrangling, CDISC, SAS, AI-assisted
  coding, and clinical-trial case studies.
- *Statistical Computing in the Age of AI* (this book)
  covers the methods in two halves, one per quarter, and
  is printed in two volumes. The first half covers
  programming in R, numerical algorithms, simulation, the
  bootstrap, and the core models (linear models, GLMs,
  mixed models, survival). The second half covers
  numerical stability, numerical linear algebra in depth,
  advanced optimization, EM, Monte Carlo, Bayesian
  computation and MCMC, parallel and high-performance
  computing, high-dimensional methods, machine learning
  for biostatistics, package development and software
  engineering, and interactive visualization.
- [*Applied Generative AI for Health Sciences Research*](https://applied-genai.rgtlab.org)
  treats generative AI as the orthogonal axis: capability
  classes, reasoning models, biomedical RAG, multimodal
  medical AI, agents and the Model Context Protocol,
  evaluation, safety, regulation, and deployment.

Together the three books form a two-year graduate
biostatistics curriculum, although each can be read
independently.

## Acknowledgments

The structural conventions of this book follow the model
used in the Posit open-source textbook series
[@wickham2023r4ds; @wickham2023rpkgs; @wickham2019advr].
These conventions include the chapter-opening diagnostic
quiz, the end-of-chapter answers, and the section-level
exercises. *Bayesian Data Analysis* and *Statistical
Rethinking* shaped the Bayesian chapters of the second half.
*Mastering Shiny* and *ggplot2* informed its visual-design
decisions. The tidyverse R packages maintained by the Posit
engineering team are used throughout the code examples, and
their consistent interface is reflected in the style of the
prose.

The content rests on the foundational work of numerous
authors in statistical computing. We note in particular the
work of Efron and Tibshirani [@efron1993bootstrap] on the
bootstrap, Bates and colleagues [@bates2015lme4] on `lme4`,
Golub and Van Loan [@golub2013matrix] on matrix
computations, and Nocedal and Wright
[@nocedal2006numerical] on optimization. Remaining errors
are the authors'.

The graduate students who engaged with early drafts of this
material contributed materially to it. They did so through
their questions and through their willingness to debate the
appropriate role of large language models in a statistics
curriculum.
